# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# A Critical Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up (VC-2023-04-F)

This follow-up settles several questions left open by the earlier documents:
- **Durability.** The Varden gain shrinks but doesn't vanish over 24 months.
- **The duration claim.** The meta-analysis's "no decay" rested on uncontrolled studies that used scheduled hours.
- **Counter work.** The county abandoned the reduced schedule for counter offices once it costed the extra staff needed.

Two of its central claims need more caution than the authors give them: the 8.5% gain "on the stricter measure," and the mediation result. Two features of the follow-up itself also bias the decay estimate: a contaminated control group, and a group of Halden organisations that chose whether to take part.

## Arithmetic checks

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuers | 96.8 / (34.9/40.3 = 0.866) | +11.8% ✓ |
| Decline from 9 to 24 months | (12.5 − 9.8) / 12.5 | −22%, "about a quarter" ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 ✓ |
| Counter staffing to restore output | 1 / 0.886 | +12.9%, close to the 12% stated ✓ |
| Counter cost per contact | 12% more staff at full pay | about +12% labour cost per contact, **not 9%** ✗ |
| Control-office meeting time | two offices fell by 2.1 hours; average fell by only 0.2 | **doesn't reconcile** ✗ |

**Counter cost.** If output is restored by adding 12% more staff, labour cost per contact rises by about 12%. The 9% figure only works if non-staff costs make up roughly a quarter of the total. The paper should say what the 9% includes.

**Control-office meetings.** The two offices that ran a meeting audit cut 2.1 hours each, which by itself would lower the control average by about 0.6 hours. Yet the average fell only from 7.2 to 7.0. Either the other five control offices added about half an hour of meetings each, or the figures are measured at different times. This needs explaining, because it is the comparison behind the mediation result.

## What the follow-up resolves

1. **"Entirely an artifact" is refuted.** The 24-month estimate uses record-based output, randomised comparison, a two-year horizon and a second hours measure, the standards Varga & Holm themselves set. It still finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8).
2. **The meta-analysis's duration claim is undercut.** The authors confirm what I suspected about the four long studies: all were uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. The benchmark for them should therefore have been about +17–19%, and +14% looks like decay rather than its absence.
3. **The energy extrapolation fails.** At 24 months, fatigue is still 0.34 SD better than control, and the per-hour gain is clearly positive. Varga & Holm's projection that energy would return to baseline by month ten does not hold.
4. **The baseline gap is filled.** At baseline, treated and control offices had similar meeting time (7.4 and 7.2 hours). That removes the concern I raised that the month-6 meetings snapshot might reflect chance imbalance.
5. **Counter work is confirmed as a loss.** After 12 months, waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, restoring service would need about 12% more staff, and the county reversed the change. That is about as clear a real-world verdict as a trial can give.

## Problems

### 1. Log-in time measures a different thing, so it isn't a "stricter" measure

The system logs record time spent working on cases. They don't record meetings, email or other work done off the system. So they measure **time spent on cases**, not total working hours. That causes three problems:

- **The paper's comparison doesn't work.** Saying logs "show slightly more work" than timesheets compares percentage changes in two different quantities.
- **Off-system work is still invisible.** The concern was unrecorded work, and the logs capture only the part of it done on the case system.
- **It changes what the mediation result means.** Cutting meetings frees time for cases, which raises output per *total* hour. It doesn't obviously raise output per *case-work* hour. If meetings explain 47% of a gain in output per hour spent on cases, the mechanism must be something like fewer interruptions or less fragmented days, not simply time freed up.

The figures also don't fit together. Suppose case-work time were total time minus meetings. Then cutting meetings by 3.5 hours while cutting total time by about 4.5 hours would shrink case-work time by only around 3%, not 11%. That suggests the logs capture something other than pure case work, perhaps time logged in to the system including idle time. The paper needs to say exactly what "active log-in time" measures. Until it does, I'd treat +8.5% and +9.8% as two estimates with different flaws, not as a strict one and a loose one.

### 2. The control-group contamination biases the decay estimate

Two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings from month 15, and their output per hour then rose by 4.1%. If offices are weighted equally, that alone lifts the control average by roughly 1 percentage point over months 16 to 24. That is enough to explain about a third to half of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8%.

Three things follow:
- **The paper needs a sensitivity analysis** that excludes the two offices, or models their change explicitly. Without it, the size of the decay is uncertain.
- **Even the direction of decay is uncertain.** The intervals at 9 and 24 months overlap heavily, and the difference between them is never tested.
- **The 4.1% figure has its own weaknesses.** It is a before-and-after comparison in two offices with no comparison group. It may also reflect regression to the mean if those offices started an audit because their performance was poor.

### 3. The mediation test is less independent and less precise than it appears

- **The data probably overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.** The test was registered at month 11, after the exploratory correlation had been seen. If the "larger sample of office-months" includes months 1 to 9, part of the test reuses the data that suggested it.
- **There are still only 14 independent units.** Months within an office are not independent observations. With 7 offices per arm, a confidence interval of 28% to 66% looks narrow. I raised the same small-sample concern about the 9-month estimates, and the paper doesn't say whether it has been addressed.
- **Mediated shares are unstable when the total effect is small.** With a total effect of 3.4% to 13.8%, the share explained can swing widely. In absolute terms, meetings account for about 4 percentage points of the 8.5, fatigue for about 1.5, and about 3 are unexplained.
- **Causal identification is weak.** The authors acknowledge that meetings weren't randomised. Offices with stronger managers may both cut more meetings and improve output for other reasons.

Even with these caveats, a registered test that recovers a substantial meetings effect is meaningful. It is far stronger evidence than the r = 0.71 across seven offices. Varga & Holm's dismissal looks premature, but the share should be stated as "roughly half, imprecisely," not 47%.

### 4. "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the categories

The marketing agency that reverted, citing client deadlines, falls in the meta-analysis's *discretionary* category. Grouping "client deadlines" with "coverage of opening hours" makes the split between work types look cleaner than it is. One discretionary organisation in eleven reverting, with output around 88 to 91, is a useful reminder: deadline-bound work with lumpy external demand can behave like coverage work.

### 5. The Halden subset is selected at several stages

The authors are candid that the continuing organisations are "survivors twice over." It is actually more than twice:
1. they enrolled voluntarily;
2. they didn't withdraw;
3. they submitted records;
4. 14 of the 23 agreed to follow-up;
5. they continued the schedule.

The +11.8% is an upper bound, as the authors say. It should not be read as evidence that the gain *grew* from the +10.8% found in the six-month correction. It is also worth noting that a Halden author co-wrote this report, although the Halden conclusions it reaches are appropriately modest.

### 6. Issues carried over from earlier

- **Cost per case is still missing.** Timesheet hours fall by about 12%, to about 33.4 a week against a schedule of 30, which suggests overtime may be continuing. Whether it is paid, and what each case now costs, is still not reported. With output per employee at −3.4% at full pay, unit labour cost has risen by at least 3.5% before any overtime.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still isn't adjusted for the fewer scheduled days.
- **Quality.** Overturn rates are still shown as levels with no confidence interval.

## Where the evidence now stands, across all five documents

**Well supported:**
- **Discretionary work, per hour.** Under randomised conditions, output per actual hour rises by about **+8–10%**, sustained to 24 months. It declines modestly from about +12.5% at nine months, though the size of the decline is uncertain because of contamination.
- **Discretionary work, per employee.** Output per employee falls by about **−3%**, so unit labour cost rises slightly at full pay.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Output per employee falls by about **−9 to −11%**. Service worsens, restoring it costs about 9–12% more per contact, and in practice organisations reverse the change.
- **Measurement.** Headline figures of more than 20% come from scheduled hours, manager ratings and uncontrolled designs.

**Moderately supported:**
- **Mechanism.** Fewer recurring meetings appears to be the largest single route, at roughly half the gain, with fatigue playing a smaller part.
- **Meetings without the hours cut.** Some of the gain may be available by cutting meetings alone. Whether the hours cut is needed to *force* that change and make it stick is untested. That would require a trial arm that reorganises without reducing hours.

**Rejected by the evidence:**
- The claim that reduced hours suit every sector (Halden).
- The claim that the gain is entirely an artifact (Varga & Holm).
- The claim that there is no decay (the meta-analysis).

**Still open:**
- What the system logs actually measure.
- Contamination-adjusted estimates of decay.
- Cost per unit of output, including overtime.
- Evidence from the private sector and manufacturing.
- Effects beyond 24 months.
